# ADR 0002 — Synthetic generation, no admin UI, and deferred deal intelligence

Date: 2026-09-23
Status: Accepted

Three decisions taken together because they share one principle: the artifacts this project is
judged on are versioned, reviewable, and reproducible. Anything that moves state outside that
boundary is rejected regardless of how convenient it looks.

## 1. All data is synthetic, generated by a generic profile-driven generator

**Decision.** The project ships no real data, ever. Data is produced by a generator that takes a
schema plus a *profile spec* and emits rows satisfying it — distributions, null rates, cardinality,
date ranges, referential integrity, and deliberately placed anomalies.

The generator is **not** a GTM-specific script. The domain shape lives in configuration; the
generator is generic.

**Why generic.** Profiling and generation are the same capability pointed in opposite directions.
The planned schema-profiling feature infers what an unfamiliar column means from its statistical
signature. A generator consumes that same signature and produces data matching it. Building the
generator generically now means an adopter can later point it at their own warehouse, obtain
synthetic data with their shape and none of their numbers, and evaluate this architecture without
exposing anything. Most organizations cannot share real GTM data with a demo, a vendor, or a job
candidate — which makes this the difference between an architecture they can try and one they
cannot.

**The anomalies are the point.** Generated data must contain, deliberately and by record:

- bookings with no corresponding billing
- bookings with no recognized revenue
- a NULL segment that must survive aggregation
- a territory reassignment falling mid-quarter
- a booking on the exact final day of a quarter
- perpetual deals recognizing at point of sale beside subscription deals recognizing ratably

These are not noise. They are the ground truth the evaluation measures against, so each is placed
intentionally and its location recorded. An agent that writes an INNER JOIN drops the orphans and
reports that everything reconciles — a false answer shaped like good news, which is the most
dangerous shape an analytics error takes. The seeded orphans are what make that detectable.

**Consequence.** The generator is a first-class component with its own tests, not a fixture script.
Determinism is required: a fixed seed and integer arithmetic only, so the same inputs always yield
byte-identical output and the ground truth cannot drift underneath the eval.

## 2. No administrative web UI. Configuration stays in git.

**Decision.** There will be no web interface for editing metric contracts, personas, or any other
configuration. All of it remains versioned YAML, reviewed as diffs.

**Why.** The integrity claim is that the evaluation spec was committed before the data models
existed, and a test asserts that ordering against git history. Contracts, questions, and reference
SQL are load-bearing precisely because they are commits — attributable, ordered, reviewable, and
impossible to revise retroactively without the revision itself being visible.

A web form that edits contracts writes state outside that history. It would be a feature that
quietly dismantles the property the project exists to demonstrate. Contracts-as-code is not a
limitation to be smoothed over with a GUI; it is the mechanism.

**Consequence.** Adopters configure this the way they configure dbt: in files, in version control,
through pull requests. That is a deliberate constraint and is stated as such rather than apologized
for.

## 3. A read-only viewer is in scope. A GTM dashboard is not.

**Decision.** One page: ask a single question, see three answer cards side by side — one per
persona — each showing its own SQL, metric versions, lineage, role and policies in effect,
`why_not`, and query ID.

**Why that page and no other.** The answer card is inherently visual. In a terminal it reads as
noise; rendered, it communicates governance, auditability, and refusal-as-a-result in one screen.
Same question, three different correct answers, each showing what it was not permitted to see — no
dashboard makes that argument more efficiently, and adoption depends on a reader reaching that
realization quickly.

**What is explicitly out of scope:** pipeline charts, funnel views, drill-downs, an executive GTM
overview. Those are BI tool territory, would be done worse here, and are unrelated to the thesis.
Anyone can render a revenue chart. Almost nobody can render one that proves who was permitted to
see it.

**Timing and stack.** The viewer is a view over the answer card, so it cannot precede one. It
follows the core. It reuses the pattern already proven in a sibling project — FastAPI, static HTML,
Docker, deployed by GitHub Actions — rather than introducing a new stack.

## 4. Deal intelligence is deferred to a separate product

**Decision.** Pipeline scoring, external and social signal enrichment, and deal-close strategy
recommendation are **not** part of this repository. They are a later, separate product that
consumes this one.

**Why deferred rather than rejected.** A cross-vendor review was unanimous on the reasoning. "Best
close strategy" has no deterministic ground truth, so it cannot be scored the way "Q3 revenue by
region" can. Placing it here would give the repository two value propositions — one provable, one
not — and reviewers would follow the more exciting story while the defensible one became a
footnote. Worse, the architecture treats non-determinism as a bug: the same question returning a
different answer on Tuesday, with no audit trail, is precisely what this exists to prevent. Deal
scoring would have to treat that as a feature.

On competing directly: the incumbents' moat is a data flywheel — call recordings, integration
depth, models tuned on closed deals — and the enrichment layer is held by LinkedIn, 6sense, and
ZoomInfo. There is no wedge on their ground for a solo builder.

**Why it is nonetheless a sequel and not a dead end.** There is one thing the incumbents do not
offer: an auditable score. Gong tells a rep a deal is at risk and cannot show why. A deal
intelligence product built *on top of* this layer inherits the answer card — every score citing its
SQL, its metric versions, its query ID. "Explainable deal scoring, every number traceable" is a real
differentiator against black-box tools.

It only works if the audited analytics layer exists first. Built together, neither gets finished.

**Consequence.** Recorded here as a deliberate deferral with its reasoning, so that revisiting it
later is a decision made against stated grounds rather than a rediscovery.
